echoes.note: Paul gathers sticks, a viper fastens on his hand, yet he shakes it off unharmed. The promise that the righteous one 'will tread on the adder' and trample serpent and viper without harm (LXX Ps 90:13) is the closest scriptural template for the scene: deadly snake, divine protection, no injury. The vocabulary of viper/serpent and the motif of the protected servant give strong thematic coherence at the book's climax.

The protoevangelium's enmity between humanity and the serpent — the serpent striking at the heel/hand while the human ultimately prevails — resonates with Paul's hand bitten yet the creature destroyed in the fire. Reversal of the primal serpent-bite is figurally apt for the apostle's vindication.

The fiery serpents that bit Israel in the wilderness and the bronze serpent of deliverance supply a background motif of snakebite and divinely-granted survival; verbal overlap is slight, link is thematic.
The wilderness journey 'with its fiery serpents' from which God preserved Israel parallels the survivor of shipwreck preserved from the venomous bite; a faint provision-and-protection echo.

Deuterocanonical reflection on Numbers 21: God's people bitten by serpents are healed not by what they saw but by God the Savior, while their bites were not fatal because of divine mercy. The pattern of harmless venom for the righteous coheres with Paul shaking off the viper unharmed.

Paul enters in to the sick father of Publius, prays, lays hands on him and heals him; the Elisha pattern of a prophet entering the sickroom and praying for restoration supplies a background healing-narrative template, with the further healings of all the island's sick recalling the prophet's wider miracles.

The islanders 'honored us with many honors' and stocked the ship with provisions; the prophetic vision of the isles/coastlands bringing their wealth and gifts to God's servants offers a faint figural resonance with Gentiles honoring the apostolic party.

When the Roman brothers come to meet him 'Paul thanked God and took courage'; the recurrent OT exhortation to 'be strong and take courage' before entering the appointed place colors his renewed resolve on arrival at Rome, though the verbal link is general.

Paul declares he is bound 'because of the hope of Israel.' The phrase 'hope of Israel' is a direct Jeremianic title for the LORD ('O hope of Israel, its savior in time of trouble'), giving real verbal coherence to Paul's self-defense.
A second Jeremianic occurrence — 'O LORD, the hope of Israel' — reinforces the title behind Paul's claim; recurrence of the phrase across Jeremiah strengthens the allusion.

The climactic citation that seals the book: 'Go to this people and say, In hearing you will hear but not understand... lest they turn and I would heal them.' Acts 28:26-27 reproduces LXX Isaiah 6:9-10 almost verbatim, explicitly attributed ('the Holy Spirit spoke rightly through Isaiah the prophet'). Maximal volume and an introductory formula — the keystone quotation.

'The salvation of God is sent to the nations' echoes the Servant commission to be 'a light to the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth' — a programmatic Isaianic text Luke uses elsewhere; here it interprets the turn to the Gentiles immediately after the Isaiah 6 hardening oracle.

'That your way may be known on earth, your saving power among all nations' (LXX Ps 66:3) supplies the universal-salvation idiom behind 'the salvation of God is sent to the nations... they will also listen.'
'All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God' reinforces the Gentile-salvation declaration; the phrase 'salvation of God' coheres closely with Paul's closing words.
'The LORD has made known his salvation... all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God' is another psalmic source for the 'salvation of God' to the nations motif behind v.28.

Paul's unhindered preaching of the Kingdom of God in the imperial capital, with all who come received, gives a faint figural fulfillment of the nations streaming to learn God's ways; the link is thematic, not verbal.
